page: The Microsoft Azure FX32-8ms_v2 is a specialized virtual machine configuration engineered for memory-intensive workloads that require high single-thread processor frequency. Built on the x86_64 architecture, it is powered by an Intel Xeon 8573C processor operating at 4.2 GHz. The instance provisions 8 dedicated virtual CPUs derived from 4 physical cores using hyperthreading, backed by 260 MB of L3 cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and advanced instruction sets including Intel AMX and AVX-512. It contains 672.0 GB of system memory, producing an expansive memory allocation of 84.0 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include local ephemeral storage or integrated GPUs, relying entirely on remote managed disks for persistence.

Empirical benchmark data reveals exceptional single-threaded performance driven by the 4.2 GHz clock speed and large cache hierarchy. The FX32-8ms_v2 lands in the top tier for Geekbench single-core performance (score of 2369.0) and text processing (score of 2937.0). It also demonstrates strong single-threaded throughput in data compression, reaching 34.8 GB/sec in gzip and 14.36 GB/sec in bzip3 decompression. In contrast, multi-core benchmarks such as the PassMark CPU score (15780.91) and multi-threaded stress-ng metrics (8881.34) reflect mid-tier throughput, bounded directly by the 8 vCPU limit. Memory throughput benchmarks show 72.43 GB/sec in uncached read operations, and Redis SET throughput scales to 13.15 million operations per second.

The extreme memory-to-vCPU ratio offers distinct qualitative cost advantages for software environments that are licensed on a per-core basis but demand significant physical memory footprints. Workloads that do not benefit from wide parallelization can avoid licensing excess CPU cores solely to obtain adequate memory capacity. However, because local storage is not bundled, high-IOPS applications must account for network storage overhead. The hardware profile suits large in-memory databases, relational database caching tiers, electronic design automation (EDA) tools, and memory-constrained data analysis.
